news.title: BIZARRE phrase that Trump used when he first dropped united Ireland bombshell on Catherine Connolly at Aras meeting - as senior aides reveal REAL reason 'hurt' US president decided to bring up thorny issue of Irish unity
news.text:
US president Donald Trump raised the issue of a United Ireland at his meeting with President Catherine Connolly at Áras an Uachtaráin unprompted - asking her how 'the merger' was going within minutes of their behind-the-scenes chat starting, the Mail can reveal.

The fact that the US president initiated the conversation throws fresh light on his later comments, when he told a joint press conference with Taoiseach Micheál Martin at Farmleigh in Dublin’s Phoenix Park that he would ‘love’ it if the North and the Republic were to reunite.

According to senior Government sources familiar with events at the meeting, the Irish President didn’t substantially engage in a discussion on reunification, focusing her efforts on raising the actions of the Israeli Defence Forces in the Gaza Strip.

A source told the MoS that President Trump ‘personally, proactively and without prompt’ from anyone in the room raised the matter of a United Ireland, which he then later addressed in a press conference when asked directly about his views on Irish unity.

Irish Government and US administration sources claimed last night that they believe Mr Trump’s statements were aimed at causing ‘maximum damage’ for Britain – which he has repeatedly criticised for failing to offer sufficient military or diplomatic support for his assaults on Iran.

‘We could see up close that his was a well-planned diplomatic assault designed to cause maximum damage to the British government,’ said a senior Irish Government source.

‘He dropped an absolute bombshell and it was not done without forethought and discussion within his administration.’

A US administration source confirmed that Mr Trump’s statements were preplanned. 

‘He has made no secret at his disappointment – hurt really – at the UK’s lukewarm support on Iran and on other foreign affairs matters,’ said the US government source, ‘and if this causes the UK difficulty, which the reaction shows it has, then maybe that’s not unintentional.’

The US president’s whistle-stop tour of Ireland started at 8.23am yesterday morning when Air Force One touched down at Dublin Airport amid one of the largest security operations the country has ever mounted.

Mr Trump, who is in Ireland principally to attend the Irish Open, being hosted at his golf resort in Doonbeg, Co. Clare, first met with President Catherine Connolly and the Taoiseach for a quick-fire round of diplomatic engagements. 

He also gave a speech to lawmakers and business leaders at the US ambassador’s residence in the Phoenix Park before flying to Doonbeg.

But it was his comments on a United Ireland that made global headlines. 

Responding to a press question about his personal views on Irish unity in Farmleigh during a meeting with Mr Martin, Mr Trump said he did not ‘want to cause any problems’ but he would ‘love to see it unified’.

He said: ‘I have friends on both sides, great people. They’re Irish people. How can they be bad, right?

‘I’d love to see it unified. I think it would be a great feather in everybody’s cap if that happened. It’s going to happen eventually.

‘You know what? The way I look at it, it’s going to happen eventually. It may as well happen now.’

Referring to the Taoiseach sitting next to him, Mr Trump added: ‘We’re talking about it and you got the right man over here to get it moving. But, yeah, I think it would be a fantastic thing.

‘Now the UK will have something to say about it, obviously. But I think it would be a great thing. I mean, how can it be bad?’

Earlier, President Trump himself had brought up a United Ireland unprompted when asked how his meeting with the Irish President had gone.

‘We did discuss Northern Ireland. I always find it to be a very interesting discussion. People of Northern Ireland and people of Ireland. They sometimes say “hey,

when are you guys getting together?” I do ask that question every time.’

Mr Martin responded: ‘You do, you’re consistent on that.’

The US president added: ‘I’m sure it’s complicated. But life is complicated.’

The remarks were swiftly responded to by all sides in the North, including the hardline unionist DUP, and by a Downing Street spokesman.

Mr Trump later discussed his comments at length at the start of his speech at Deerfield, the US ambassador’s residence.

He addressed his comments to a room that included Mr Martin, his wife Mary, Irish Ambassador to the US Geraldine Nason-Byrne, financial tycoon Dermot Desmond and fellow billionaire Denis O’Brien.

Referring to the question that had been asked earlier in Farmleigh, the US president said: ‘But they’re going for the kill at all times, and they ask me a question: “What do you think about unification of Northern Ireland and Ireland?’’ 

'I said: “Oh, that’s a nice question.” I gave a nice answer, I think. We’ll read about it tomorrow.

‘That’s one of those questions where, no matter what you say, no matter how well you say it, there’s no good answer, right?

‘But I actually said it would be, I think, a very cool thing. To be honest with you, I think it would be cool. As half the room clears out, they say: “Let’s get the hell out of here. I don’t like this guy. I liked him a lot 10 minutes ago. I don’t like him”.’

Crucially the Government did not interpret these later remarks as an effort to row back.

Indeed, those closest to the stage felt that President Trump was ‘gleefully’ revelling in the knowledge that he had just thrown a ‘hand grenade’ in Irish public affairs. 

The MoS was standing just feet from President Trump during the speech, and it was clear that he was enjoying his unrivalled ability to grab headlines.

The subject of a United Ireland has moved up the political agenda this year, with Fine Gael moving to publish a green paper on Irish unity later this year. 

And the new UK prime minister Andy Burnham sparked a political row last month when he said a unity referendum was ‘off the table’.

Mr Martin has edged closer to calling for a border poll recently, telling reporters at the party’s think-in this week that it was his view that it was ‘not satisfactory’ that a decision to call a referendum was left as a ‘judgement call’ for the Northern Ireland secretary. 

He said that there ‘needs to be a discussion’ about how a referendum would be triggered.

However, Mr Martin himself dodged reporters’ questions on Mr Trump’s remarks as he left Farmleigh to travel to the US ambassador’s residence.

Later, a spokesman for the Taoiseach said President Trump’s comments on a United Ireland ‘should come as a surprise to no one’.

‘Over the years the president has been consistent in his view that he sees unity in Ireland as the optimal outcome.’

The spokesman said that, over the past two years in the White House, the president expressed this to the Taoiseach, and on Capitol Hill this year.

‘The Taoiseach told the President that he leads a party that supports Irish unity.

‘He also outlined the work of the Shared Island initiative and the importance of creating stronger communities and shared experiences on the island.’

‘The Taoiseach highlighted Ireland’s significant experience in conflict resolution as a result of the peace process, and that this experience could be brought to bear in the Middle East or other conflict areas.’

He said President Trump was very aware of how violent the conflict in Northern Ireland was, and of the importance of peace.

‘The Taoiseach paid tribute to successive US governments for their role in the peace process and in helping bring about the Good Friday Agreement.’

Tánaiste Simon Harris said the comments showed ‘how much the conversation about a unified island is advancing at home and abroad’, adding: ‘As you know, I made it clear that Fine Gael would produce a blueprint for a unified island. 

'That work is progressing well and we will produce our output and next steps at our Ard Fheis.’

A spokesman for No. 10 referred to comments by prime minister Burnham in the House of Commons last week where he said he would ‘stick to it [the Good Friday Agreement] 100 per cent’.

On Wednesday Mr Burnham had said that the question of a border poll was for the Northern Ireland secretary, ‘when there is a clear consensus in the country – when public opinion has changed to the point at which the call has to be considered’.

The leader of Sinn Féin, Mary Lou McDonald would only ‘acknowledge’ the comments from Mr Trump.

She said: ‘I acknowledge President Trump’s comments on the reunification of Ireland.

‘The conversation on Irish unity has shifted, and the onus is on the Taoiseach to begin planning. 

'We have secured peace, and as we approach the thirtieth anniversary of the Good Friday Agreement, our national journey is now reunification, which is organised, planned and a peaceful transition.’

The party was involved in some of the protests against the US president’s visit to Ireland over the weekend.

The US president’s comments also prompted a quick response from the DUP, with party leader Gavin Robinson tweeting: ‘President Trump knows better than most that elections matter. 

'Northern Ireland’s constitutional future will be decided by the people of Northern Ireland, not by commentary in London, Dublin or Washington.’

‘Northern Ireland is part of the United Kingdom because that is the settled democratic will of its people,’ he added.

And Gregory Campbell, a DUP MP from Derry, said he didn’t know what was behind the comments by President Trump, speculating they may have been related to Catherine Connolly, who has been a strong critic of Mr Trump and US foreign policy.

He added: ‘I mean, if this wasn’t for real, this would make a Father Ted episode.

Colum Eastwood, the former leader of the SDLP and an MP for the party, tweeted ‘always liked him’ in response to Mr Trump’s comments about Irish unity.

He came, he saw, he watched the golf: Trump keeping low profile in Doonbeg

Trump, an avid golf fan, made a whistle-stop political tour before heading for Clare. 

11.20pm, 12 Sep 2026

Share options

DONALD TRUMP’S ARRIVAL at his Doonbeg golf course today was done in spectacular fashion, with Irish Open attendees treated to an Air Force One fly-by shortly before 2pm ahead of the US President touching down. 

Hundreds of golf fans turned their back on the game as they waited for Trump’s Marine One helicopter to land on the helipad a short distance from where Shane Lowry was putting. 

The Journal / YouTube

Lowry played on as Trump’s helicopter flew into view, an hour after the Air Force One flyby.

Just before Trump’s helicopter landed, two military Chinooks, one carrying the US press pool, and a second USA-emblazoned helicopter also touched down at the golf resort. 

Trump was quickly whisked into the waiting motorcade, which brought him and his entourage up to the hotel, without the waiting spectators catching even a glimpse of the president.

Trump applauds Rory McIlroy as he finishes his round at the Irish OpenAlamy

From there, he and his two sons, Eric and Donald Jnr, made their way to a designated private viewing platform for the US president at the 18th green, where the president spent the rest of the afternoon, engrossed in the golf.

Just outside the viewing platform, an armoured, bulletproof golf buggy sat waiting to transport the US president around the course. 

Speaking to The Journal, one of the DP World Tour organisers said that they had “never seen anything” like the security operation that was underway at the five-star resort. 

Advertisement

Trump's armoured golf buggy.The Journal

The Journal

But despite the heavy security and flashy entrance, the US president’s presence at the golf tournament was relatively low-key, with little fanfare from spectators who largely seemed to take the president and his entourage in their stride. 

While Irish media waited outside the entrance to the private viewing platform, hoping to get a question or two to Trump, young boys were also lingering, but their focus was on collecting autographs, gloves and golf balls from the pro-players, not seeing the US president. 

Trump spent hours watching the golf on Saturday afternoon.Alamy

A half-hour drive away in Doonbeg village, a small group of peaceful protesters had gathered for the day to voice their disapproval of the US president’s visit. 

Nearby Shannon Airport, peaceful protesters also gathered, many of them with Palestinian flags.

In Doonbeg on Saturday evening, the mood was jovial. People spilt out from the pubs, and music played over loudspeakers from the Doonbeg Fáilte Fest, which was organised to coincide with the Irish Open. 

Mixed among festival-goers was a small group of Trump protesters, carrying placards with phrases like “Stop Supporting Genocide”, “Gaza is not 4 sale” and “No US Planes No War”.

By the time The Journal spoke to them on the village’s main street at around 7.30pm, they were tired and packing up for the day, but still good-tempered despite the somewhat hostile response from some of the crowd.

Trump protesters in Doonbeg village on Saturday eveningThe Journal

The Journal

As The Journal spoke to one Trump protest, a man in a car passing by rolled down his window and shouted: “Up Trump!” 

A few moments later, a group of young men walking past with their takeaway chips jeered at the protesters as one of the young men filmed them. 

One of the protesters, Sarah Clancy, said the group was unperturbed: the general response across the day had been positive. 

Clancy, a community worker in Clare, said there were a lot of reasons she was protesting Trump’s visit, but top of the list was the situations in Gaza and Lebanon.

Eric Trump promises a ballroom for Doonbeg and a Trump Tower for Dublin in RTÉ interview

“We are in a village here of about 200 people, and Israel, supported by Trump, has cleared nearly 100 villages across Lebanon… Places just like this, where people have made their lives for decades,” Clancy said. 

“If it were me, I would like to think people would come out and support me, and not be rolling out the red carpet [for Donald Trump].” 

She added: “The place I would like to see him welcomed is the International Criminal Court.

Melina Sharp, another protester, said she has gone to numerous protests at Shannon Airport against Donald Trump. 

Like Clancy, a key focus for her was the genocide in Gaza and Israel and the US’s war on Iran.

“That guy [Trump] is financing and pushing genocides and illegal wars. He should have no place in Ireland,” Sharp said.

Meanwhile, back at the Trump International Hotel, Rory McIlroy confirmed to reporters that he would be having dinner with the US President, who was later spotted walking through the hotel’s packed residents’ bar as punters sang Fields of Athenry, Grace and Sweet Caroline.

One property owner on Doonbeg's main street was not shy about who they were backing in the Irish Open.The Journal

The Journal

The US President appeared relaxed across the afternoon in Doonbeg, almost laser-focused on the golf. 

So much so that you would almost forget that earlier in the day he sparked a diplomatic row after he supported a united Ireland during a press conference with Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

In Dublin, Irish political leaders will have exhaled a sigh of relief that the political element of Trump’s visit is now down, and those comments were the most consequential element of the trip.

Meanwhile, down in Doonbeg, whether the US president will keep as low a profile on the final day of the Irish Open tomorrow as he did today is anyone’s guess.

news.title: Flatley playing the flute, An Taoiseach and Dermot Desmond chatting animatedly, and exactly why Trump called the Irish 'vicious bastards' - John Lee brings you behind the scenes at the Ambassador's reception
news.text:
My invite from US Ambassador Ed Walsh to attend ‘an address by President Donald J Trump’ intriguingly told me to show up at the Garda Boat Club, at Islandbridge, on the River Liffey, between 6am and 8am on Saturday morning.

Since it arrived by email at 22.12 on Wednesday evening, the obscure references to a pre–daylight – later clarified to 6.15am – rendezvous, with no ultimate destination, made it all excitedly cloak and dagger.

The invite ended: ‘US Embassy will provide transportation… to the event location.’

Since the Irish Mail on Sunday had broken the story that President Trump was to come to Ireland, I had leaned on some US contacts to get an invite to one of his private events. I had gotten to know US Ambassador Ed Walsh since he became a member of my golf club – the Island Golf Club – and had interviewed him. And I asked him last week for access.

So I’m assuming that it was Ambassador Walsh who ratified our behind–the–scenes look at ‘Trump in Ireland’ but I still don’t know for sure.

Further information did arrive on Friday and I found myself walking into the Garda Boat Club car park in the pitch dark at 6am.

Buses were lined up. On the bus seat in front of me were Senator Gerard Craughwell and former TD Cathal Berry and beside me was a large gentleman faintly smelling of his previous night’s revelry.

It might not have been early for these former Army men but it was for others.

Still, although I’d gotten some indication from the Daily Mail’s Washington desk that President Trump would come to work a room at Deerfield, and then give a speech to business leaders and US Embassy staff, nobody on the bus seemed to know for sure what time Trump would arrive or what he would do.

When we rolled into Deerfield, the magnificent US Ambassador’s Residence in the Phoenix Park, at 6.10am, it was still dark.

After we got off the bus, we were pointed through driving rain, across the lawn to a huge marquee.

The American guests felt at home as their uniquely awful coffee was on tap with some flimsy pastries. Business attire had been recommended but many of the women guests – there were a lot more men than women – were in borderline ballroom dress and didn’t look chuffed at what was looking like a long wait.

I, however, as a veteran of many visits with taoisigh to the US knew, that along with bad coffee, US governments like to give you a long wait, to drive home the importance of the administration official you are waiting for.

I have stood on a freezing White House lawn a few times for over an hour, once spent many hours on a hard floor in the freezing Eisenhower Executive Office Building (next to the White House), waited in a collapsing tent on the lawn of the residence of the US Vice President and many other venues, for many hours, for never–explained reasons. That we stood around in an even larger marquee next door to the catering one for five hours doing nothing is par for the course.

A duo with a guitar and a banjo eventually got on the stage and banged out Irish standards and comedian Alan Shortt was our MC. A young female soprano sang The Star–Spangled Banner and Mr Shortt interviewed Michael Flatley who then played the flute.

He has a spectacular collection of flutes at home in Castlehyde, a fellow guest told me.

The room had filled with business leaders from companies like Microsoft, Amazon, CRH, Saville and the banking sector. There were a number of former politicians who have gone onto business and consulting. 

Former Fine Gael ministers Lucinda Creighton, Simon Coveney, Brian Hayes and former FG TD John Deasy were there. Rockwell Consulting and former Labour senator Lorraine Higgins was in the 200–strong crowd too, along with businessmen Ian Hyland and Declan Ganley.

A smattering of TDs and senators looked to have been there from very early. The labels on the small number of white chairs surrounding the stage revealed some were for business executives while in the box seats were Taoiseach Micheál Martin and his wife Mary. 

To Mr Martin’s left sat US Ambassador Geraldine Byrne Nason and to her left were billionaires, Dermot Desmond and Denis O’Brien. The seating message was clear – alongside our important politician were the tycoons, and the Taoiseach spent some time in animated conversation with Mr Desmond as we waited for Trump.

Word came in from Dublin Airport that Donald Trump had wearily and stiffly descended the steep staircase to ask Tánaiste Simon Harris what he ‘thought’ of ‘my new plane’. Mr Harris told him it was ‘certainly a very big one’.

There were what Irish Government sources described as ‘strenuous’ efforts made by the US Administration overnight to move the earlier Micheal Martin–Donald Trump bilateral meeting from the Farmleigh official residence to the Deerfield US Ambassador’s Residence. 

These efforts were successfully resisted and the US Administration had to settle for just the president speaking.

At around 11.40am Mr and Mrs Martin took their seats alongside Mr Desmond and Mr O’Brien.

Cabinet members also took their seats to the left of the stage, alongside Donald Trump Jnr and his wife Bettina. Seated behind them, Trump’s controversial aide Natalie Harp could be seen.

US Ambassador Ed Walsh, a close friend and golf partner of Trump, was the final warm–up act and then came the Big Man at 11.50am.

Trump, wearing a two–tone, red striped tie came out to the mournful MAGA dirge God Bless the USA and stood alone, still and silent for a few minutes, mindful of his image for the cameras.

I’ve heard him speak many times, and attended many of his press conferences and Oval Office events, so the themes and rambling, structureless style are very familiar. He was effusive about Ireland and the Irish people and a Cabinet minister later told me this alone could not be bought on the budgets provided to Bord Fáilte and other State agencies.

He can be genuinely funny, Trump, and his casual, scattergun style is engaging, mostly because you can’t drop into complete somnolence because he will, eventually, say something outrageous.

He is not completely without an emotional intelligence for what the crowd wants either. The crowd had at times laughed with real warmth at some of his jokes – his reference to Irish people as ‘vicious b*****ds’ was taken in that jocular spirit – and guffawed performatively for his less funny material.

But when he turned to insulting the ill Joe Biden, who has long left the political scene, there was silence. Sensing that he was slagging off an Irish American admired in this room, he quickly turned to criticising his ‘Communist’ opponents in the Democrat party. 

Trump moves slowly and certainly seems older and more fatigued than when I first saw him as president, up close in the Oval Office, in 2017. There is a big difference between 71 and 80 and his speaking voice is weaker and more littered with slurs than I recall it being as recently as 2025 in the Oval Office.

Then, there was a dark, almost sinister atmosphere. Here, on a breezy, balmy Dublin autumn day, there was only bonhomie and happiness.

Trump seemed comfortable and has a true warmth for Ireland.

The context of his ‘vicious b*****ds’ reference was explained to me by a business acquaintance of his who I met in the crowd.

‘He’s talking about their hard–dealing reputation of the Mafia–dominated real estate sector in New York of the 1970s and 1980s,’ said Trump’s friend, ‘that time toughened him up and he did business with the Irish. He admires them.’

Tipperary Fine Gael TD Michael Murphy was also there, and he gave me a unique insight into Trump’s fondness for Ireland, if only of the misty, imaginary Irishness of America. 

Mr Murphy is a cousin of the late tenor Frank Patterson. Trump’s mother loved Patterson and Trump contacted the tenor to ask him to sing to her at hospital in her final days.

 Such things seep into the Trump–Ireland relationship. This trip was also a personal triumph for Ed Walsh who has forged a close relationship with, in particular, Simon Harris and Micheál Martin.

Mr Martin appeared invigorated by this brush with the US president, and the 66–year–old looked vibrant and vigorous in comparison to the lumbering Trump.

They are two masterful politicians and Mr Martin’s understanding of the sprinkling of stardust that comes with the US President – even the most controversial in history – was on show.

All the Fine Gael members of Cabinet were there but only Fianna Fáil’s Darragh O’Brien and James Lawless were seen at Deerfield yesterday.

Many noted the absence of the Fianna Fáil heir apparent, Jim O’Callaghan. I recall overhearing Mr Martin telling a recently new political mother that ‘babies are good for votes’ and I was reminded, again, that so too are US presidents.

Even Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly, who doesn’t have to stand for election, saw the value of accepting an invite. Despite the fact that in recent months he has featured regularly in these pages, and has not been left free of criticism, he came over to me to say hello and introduce himself.

When Trump finally left the stage, Mr Martin smoothly put himself between the room and the door we had all entered through.

Alongside him was Mary Martin, and you couldn’t leave the tent without taking an opportunity to shake hands or chat to the couple. 

The queue, in which I spotted many Fine Gaelers, stretched across the tent floor. Trump had long left in the limo known as The Beast – not by the Marine One helicopter as I had been briefed – and still the Taoiseach stood in the garden of the US Ambassadorial Residence shaking hands.

A few of us didn’t wait for the buses and decided to walk the two miles back to the park gate where I jumped in a taxi. 

On the taxi ride home, I got a call from a senior Government source who told me that rather than the whole United Ireland controversy blowing up accidentally, Trump had premeditated the discussion and stridently brought what he calls the ‘merger’ up in his meeting with President Catherine Connolly.

Since this was the first substantial meeting of the day, it was a wholly intentional Donald Trump–created political storm, which US and Irish officials were last night seeing as a deliberate two fingers to the UK government.

Grabbing headlines all over the world from a jaunt to see a golf tournament at his golf course is a unique skill. And despite the unofficial nature of the visit, it could yet turn out to be the most consequential of US presidential visits.

It will certainly be remembered for the political dynamite he laid.

And when political dynamite goes off, I have found that despite what Jim O’Callaghan appears to think, it is always good to be there.

 Anthropic boss calls for slowing pace of AI development 







NEW YORK, United States (AFP) — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Saturday called on artificial intelligence (AI) firms to slow down the development of the powerful technology, amid mounting worries over the risks of “superintelligent” computer systems.

His comments came a few days after AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who left OpenAI to join Anthropic, decided to leave the industry, accusing both United States (US) companies of “gambling with our lives” in the race to develop models capable of self-improvement.

“We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain,” Amodei wrote in a post on his personal website.

“AI brings risks, and because it is such a powerful technology, these risks are serious.”

“Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way,” said Amodei, who co-founded Anthropic with his sister Daniela in 2021.

“But over the last few months, I have become convinced that fully addressing the risks requires even more prudence.”

Amodei’s statement echoes another call by Anthropic in early June to slow or suspend development.

Then in late July, Sam Altman, the boss of Anthropic rival OpenAI, said developers might need to voluntarily pump the brakes on their rapid advances to give society a chance to catch up.

At roughly the same time, more than 1,000 employees at cutting-edge AI companies, including Amodei signed a petition calling on the US government to help “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

OpenAI had revealed that during testing, the AI models broke out of their confined environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site developers use to store and share code.

In that incident and others, the blame was placed on AI agents, which are software programs that can carry out tasks without constant supervision by humans.

Earlier this week, Coxon, 27, sounded the alarm after spending the past three years pretraining AI models — first at OpenAI and then, this year, at its rival Anthropic, which he considered more cautious in its approach.

Pretraining is the stage where AI models absorb vast quantities of data.

“Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon said Tuesday.

“The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade,” he said in a post on X.

Superintelligence is the theoretical point when AI’s capabilities exceed human intelligence.

– ‘Taking over the entire internet’ –

Amodei cautioned that the Hugging Face incident should not be dismissed as a one-off.

“A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand,” he explained.

“Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” potentially generating hundreds of billions of dollars in damage, he added.

The Anthropic CEO said his company would grant “employee-like access” to a team of “third-party evaluators” who would verify adherence to safety practices — and he called on all companies to follow his lead.

He also suggested that companies work together to establish common safety standards, and said he supported some kind of government cooperation on the issue.

In early August, the US government put in place a voluntary security review process for advanced AI models before their release, but the parameters of that program remain unclear.

Industry observers say they are not sure how effective it would be, as President Donald Trump’s administration has thus far favored a light-touch, deregulatory approach to most industries, including tech.

news.title: Russian Strikes Kill 9 Across Ukraine, As Zelenskyy Offers To Meet Putin At Miami G20
news.text:
KYIV-- Russia continued to pound the Ukrainian civilian population, killing at least nine people in attacks throughout the country, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated he'd be willing to meet Russia’s Vladimir Putin at the upcoming G20 summit -- something the Kremlin called “impossible.”

Russia has intensified air strikes throughout Ukraine over the past two months, with the Kremlin hitting power plants and other infrastructure as the potentially brutal winter months loom on the horizon.

Civilian deaths were reported in several cities and regions on September 12 as Ukraine struggles to secure its population amid a shortage of air defense weapons badly needed to intercept high-speed Russian missile.

In Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, the city of some 150,000 people -- which has been under Russian military pressure for months -- local authorities said Russian forces attacked private cars, killing three people in three incidents over a 90-minute period.

"These are not ⁠military targets," the city council said in a statement. "They are ordinary civilian cars. ‌People were going about their business."

Vitaliy Bunechko, governor of Ukraine's Zhytomyr region west of Kyiv, said a Russian strike hit a grocery store, killing two people in the town of Zvyahel.

Ivan Fedorov, governor of Zaporizhzhia region, said two people were killed and 11 injured in assaults on Zaporizhzhia and other communities.

Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryviy Rih's ‌military administration, said two people had been killed in overnight attacks on the city by drones and missiles.

Russia’s military claimed its forces targeted Ukrainian steel maker Zaporizhstal in Zaporizhzhia, an Interpipe Steel complex in Dnipro, and several plants in Kryviy Rih.

The claims could not independently be verified.

In response to Russian attacks, Ukraine has hit energy facilities and warehouses, often deep inside Russia, causing acute energy shortages throughout the country, while both sides have targeted each others' shipping in and around the Black Sea.

Zelenskyy Willing To Meet In Miami

In a interview with German broadcaster Deutsche Welle released on September 12, Zelenskyy said he would be willing to meet with Putin for peace talks at the December 14-15 Group 0f 20 (G20) gathering in Miami.

"Yes, of course," he said when asked about a meeting.

"We have to come. We have to meet, to speak, and make decisions. It's not about words. What I will tell him or what he wants to tell me, it doesn't matter. Results matter."

The Kremlin immediately rejected Zelenskyy's offer.

"It is impossible," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told AFP, repeating Russia’s demand that such a face-to-face meeting could only take place in Moscow.

"There is a readiness to meet him in Moscow," said Peskov, who noted that it has not been decided yet whether Putin will attend the G20 gathering.

Zelenskyy has long rejected the possibility of meeting in Moscow at a time when his country is facing a full-scale invasion by Russian forces.

“He can come to Kyiv," Zelenskyy told ABC News in reference to Putin.

"I can't go to Moscow when my country's under missiles, under attack, each day. I can't go to the capital of this terrorist."

Washington is attempting to kick-start long-stalled talks on Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kyiv last week, while US President Donald Trump and Putin have conducted phone talks in recent days.

In the Deutsche Welle interview, which took place on September 11 while he was in Canada, Zelenskyy said Witkoff and Kushner's visit was a "good signal" and that it was important the two had made a trip to Kyiv as well as Moscow.

Zelensky has said he he plans to meet Trump in late September, although details have not been confirmed.

Trilateral Talks

Meanwhile, a top Ukrainian official suggested US-Russia-Ukraine talks could resume as early as next month.

Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian presidential office, said a new round of trilateral talks on ending the war may take place in October.

Speaking to the Interfax-Ukraine news agency on the sidelines of the Yalta European Security forum in Kyiv, Budanov said Ukraine is preparing for a new meeting in the trilateral format, but he did not provide details.

Earlier, Budanov told The New York Times that the negotiation process would likely intensify after Russia's State Duma elections on September 18–20 and the US midterm elections on November 3.

The last direct talks between Russia and Ukraine came in February in Switzerland, with the US acting as mediator and with Budanov being a part of the Ukrainian delegation.

With reporting by AFP and Reuters
news.summary: Russia continued to pound the Ukrainian civilian population, killing at least nine people in attacks throughout the country, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy repeated he'd be willing to meet Russia’s Vladimir Putin at the upcoming G20 summit -- something the Kremlin called “impossible.”

news.title: LETTER: Canada can’t trust U.S. government
news.text:
Dear Editor,

A letter to the leader of the United States and the people of the United States,

Donald Trump and his political cronies have made it personal by attacking Canada on the level of a child’s intellect with memes and insults and demands. You have not just insulted the country of Canada but its people. That’s 41,000,000-plus Canadians of all different backgrounds and ages. 41 million.

Here’s a pledge from one Canadian that any American product will be overlooked in any store I visit. Any American-made vehicle that waits to be purchased can be ignored and will acquire cobwebs before it leaves the lot. All Canadian-made and foreign-manufactured products will have the utmost priority over American-made products.

Travel is a priority for a majority of Canadians, but the United States will be no longer a consideration; we are one nation that seeks what the world offers us in freedom and security, and your country is no longer stable and secure. The United States should be shunned by all democratic societies with the ability to make free decisions.

Canadians and the world need to move away from purchasing any form of product that is stamped ‘Made in America’ or is a byproduct of the United States. If you’re buying American, you’re buying Trump’s policies and his agenda in dominating the world with his unprecedented demands and policies, and continuing insults.

Build Canadian, purchase Canadian, and support Canadian industries and businesses and their workers and our Canadian governments.

The American people need to address the problems in their government. In this Canadian’s view, your country has crossed the line, and the border between you and me is closed indefinitely. Our trust is no more with your government, and just to finish this as one Canadian with the freedom to speak, “there ain’t no sunshine in America anymore.”

Cran Campbell, Langley City

news.title: Experts Warn of Emerging Attack Threat Facing the United States
news.text:
A foreign adversary launches a coordinated assault on America’s critical infrastructure, planting stealthy malware to disrupt water and electricity networks while drones strike vital power equipment.

The consequences quickly spread. Blackouts knock out communications, payment systems and hospital services, while pumps stop transporting clean water and processing sewage. Supermarket shelves empty as supplies of food and medicine dwindle.

Within days, officials are confronted with a fast-moving emergency: infrastructure is failing, stockpiled supplies are running low and communities are becoming increasingly desperate.

Some now describe the scenario as a ‘cyber 9/11’—a long-feared threat receiving renewed attention 25 years after the September 11 attacks killed roughly 3,000 people in New York City, Washington DC and Pennsylvania.

In recent weeks, warnings have come from figures ranging from national security leaders to Silicon Valley’s most prominent artificial intelligence executives. They say the United States’ infrastructure is dangerously exposed to a coordinated attack capable of causing widespread, debilitating disruption.

Annie Fixler, a cybersecurity specialist at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD), told Our News Outlet that the “steady drumbeat” of increasingly serious warnings can no longer be dismissed.

Fixler considers major cities including New York and Los Angeles especially vulnerable to attacks targeting electricity and water networks. Such an assault, she said, could leave taps running dry within hours.

“Can you ship in enough bottled water for a large city by road? Probably not,” she said, offering a stark illustration of how quickly a critical infrastructure crisis could escalate.

“If you don’t have systems that remove wastewater, you can make a city uninhabitable in a matter of hours,” she warned, describing a threat few Americans have been forced to consider seriously.

Fixler believes China poses the most serious danger. She and other experts argue that Beijing is quietly positioning itself to disable US infrastructure ahead of a potential military operation to seize Taiwan, the self-governing island China claims as its territory.

Fresh research from her FDD colleagues, published under the title Axis of Aggressors, suggests Beijing could enlist hackers from Russia, Iran and North Korea to help pull it off.

Much of the groundwork has already been documented by investigators.

In July and August, a coordinated wave of cyber-physical attacks struck water and wastewater utilities across at least a dozen American states without warning.

Hackers targeted the small computers that control water pumps and pressure valves.

Minnesota was hit hardest, with more than 30 municipal water systems compromised by hackers in a matter of weeks.

In the small town of Braham, the entire municipal water supply was briefly knocked offline by the intruders.

US intelligence and federal investigators strongly suspect Iran is responsible, as retaliation for the conflict between Washington and Tehran that shows no signs of cooling down.

Cyber offers Tehran a cheap, asymmetric way to punch back at its mighty enemy, experts say.

Meanwhile, China has separately been exposed for covertly infecting America’s electricity, water and transport networks through a shadowy hacking group called Volt Typhoon.

Instead of using obvious computer viruses, these high-tech commandos steal passwords to blend in as normal network managers.

Traditional security systems are blind to the threat.

Analysts fear Beijing could ultimately trigger its hidden digital land mines in what is dubbed an ‘Everything, Everywhere, All at Once’ assault designed to paralyze the entire nation simultaneously.

The group was uncovered and publicly named by Microsoft alongside the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), sending shockwaves through Washington’s national security establishment.

In chilling testimony to Congress, Kevin Mandia, a top cybersecurity expert, warned that Volt Typhoon’s hackers were so stealthy that many of their American targets ‘won’t even know they’re impacted.’

Beijing has categorically denied involvement in infrastructure hacking campaigns, dismissing the accusations as an unfounded and politically motivated Western conspiracy.

Still, the devastating effectiveness of similar attacks has already been laid bare for the country to witness firsthand.

Russian ransomware hackers struck the Colonial Pipeline in May 2021, shutting down the massive 5,500-mile pipeline supplying 45 percent of the East Coast’s fuel supply for six agonizing days.

More than 10,000 gas stations across the Southeast ran dry, forcing the private operator to pay a $4.4 million ransom in Bitcoin to regain control.

Physical sabotage poses an equally terrifying threat, experts warn, and requires far less sophistication than a cyberattack does.

In April 2013, snipers fired more than 100 rounds into California’s Metcalf substation, destroying 17 transformers and narrowly avoiding a Silicon Valley blackout.

Nearly a decade later, saboteurs used high-powered rifles to blast two Duke Energy substations in North Carolina, plunging 45,000 residents into freezing darkness for days.

Jon Wellinghoff, a former chairman of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, warns that these attacks expose the grid as a fragile, domino-like system remarkably easy to topple.

Saboteurs need to only disable nine critical high-voltage substations to trigger a cascading nationwide blackout lasting up to 18 months, potentially causing societal collapse.

Identifying which substations to target is disturbingly simple, the veteran regulator turned whistleblower says.

‘It’s probably something that a bunch of 12-year-olds with the internet could do pretty easily,’ he told The New York Times in August.

Wellinghoff is not the only one sounding the alarm about America’s crumbling digital defenses.

Jen Easterly, the US Army veteran who led CISA until last year, says the country remains fundamentally unprepared for what hackers could soon unleash.

For decades, technology vendors prioritized speed-to-market and consumer convenience over basic cybersecurity safeguards, experts say.

The result is inherently insecure, defective code forming a dangerous ‘soft underbelly’ exposed to foreign military manipulation.

The US is, of course, not alone in this regard. American allies such as Britain, Australia and Taiwan are also targeted.

But the US is seen as the primary threat for such actors as Iran and China, and is especially vulnerable due to its fragmented water districts and local power grids.

Fixler told Our News Outlet that water and power grid executives she speaks with are painfully aware of their vulnerabilities.

They know about them because they’ve spent decades penny-pinching, avoiding upgrades that seemed unnecessary on any given ordinary day.

‘There are the threats that really keep people awake at night because they know they have vulnerabilities that they don’t know about,’ Fixler said grimly.

America operates nearly 150,000 public water systems, and many are tiny and run on shoestring budgets, unequipped to fend off sophisticated attacks from Chinese state hackers.

Regulators, she added, remain unprepared for a coordinated wave of enemy operatives unleashing small drones against energy substations nationwide.

Worse still, she said, the public has grown so numb to constant AI warnings that genuine dangers are increasingly dismissed with a shrug and an eye roll.

‘It’s the fault of policy experts writ large. We don’t explain why it matters to the average person,’ said Fixler, who heads FDD’s Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation.

The threat will only intensify, according to the FBI, National Security Agency and CISA, which have jointly documented how artificial intelligence is turbocharging the capabilities of malicious digital attackers worldwide.

Major technology companies issued an urgent joint warning in August that time is rapidly running out to fortify global networks against sophisticated, AI-driven cyber threats.

A coalition of 116 major technology, cybersecurity and financial firms, led by OpenAI, warned that organizations have only a narrow ‘defenders’ window’ of mere months to act.

After that window closes, they cautioned, autonomous AI-driven cyber threats would swiftly outpace existing human security measures.

The Justice Department and FBI have dramatically accelerated offensive legal and technical action against foreign state-sponsored hacking networks in recent months.

Officials in late August unsealed court documents targeting QTFY, a Chinese state-linked group accused of digital raids on NASA, the Federal Reserve and the Department of Energy.

President Donald Trump has signed multiple executive actions on technology threats, including a sweeping August 2026 emergency declaration targeting cybersecurity backdoors buried inside the US power grid.

Experts insist today’s danger looks nothing like the threat that emerged 25 years ago, when Al Qaeda terrorists hijacked passenger planes and flew them into the Pentagon and World Trade Center.

Back then, Osama bin Laden commanded a band of radicalized militants operating out of Afghanistan, a world away from today’s alleged culprit.

Beijing, by contrast, is the planet’s manufacturing powerhouse, its second-largest economy, and an increasingly formidable top-tier military superpower.

Yet the parallels remain unmistakable, experts say, since both threats exploited glaring blind spots that American security chiefs failed to see coming in time.

Al Qaeda realized hijacked planes could become deadly missiles; today’s adversaries have realized the nation’s water and power systems are society’s overlooked soft targets.

Just as locking cockpit doors might have derailed the September 11 hijackers, Fixler insists simple fixes today could dramatically shrink America’s exposure to a modern cyber 9/11.

‘We’ve left systems connected to the internet with default passwords or no passwords in place,’ she said, before delivering her blunt final verdict. ‘Let’s fix those things, and then we can worry about the apocalypse.’

news.title: Putin warns Europe against sending troops to Ukraine
news.text: Russian strikes killed eight civilians and wounded dozens of other people in Ukraine, local officials said Saturday, after Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that sending European troops into Ukraine would amount to direct conflict with Russia.Putin, speaking to reporters at a summit of the BRICS group of emerging economies in India on Friday, said that if European governments send troops into Ukraine, it will mean "a war with Russia.""Now they're talking about how they're considering sending troops into Ukraine. That means a war with Russia," he said.Some European leaders have pledged their commitment to a potential peacekeeping force, a prospect that Moscow has repeatedly described as unacceptable.Putin also denied Russia posed any threat to Europe, saying "there is no such threat and never has been.""We do not threaten, nor do we intend to threaten, European countries," he said.Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday that two incidents along Ukraine's borders with Poland and Moldova this week were a preview of potential intensified Russian provocations at Ukraine's border crossing points with Europe.Two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday night, while a "direct threat" to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point on Wednesday night was only avoided thanks to cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, he said.Ukraine, meanwhile, is under mounting pressure from Russia's intensifying air campaign that uses ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce defenses. Moscow's attacks have targeted Ukraine's power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralize civilians.Two people were killed and one wounded when Russian drones struck a residential area overnight in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia, regional head Ivan Fedorov said.One person died and three others were wounded in strikes on Kryvyi Rih, according to local officials.In the Black Sea port of Odesa and the surrounding area, 35 people were wounded overnight in what regional head Oleh Kiper called a "massive attack." Among the buildings hit was a residential high-rise, whose upper floors were completely destroyed.Three people were killed on Saturday when cars were hit by drones in Kramatorsk in Ukraine's partially occupied Donetsk region, along with a further two people in a Russian attack on a grocery store in the Zhytomyr region, local officials said.Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces struck two chemical industry facilities in Russia, one in Samara and one in Perm. The governors of the regions did not immediately comment, but Russian independent online news outlet Astra reported drone attacks on chemical plants in both regions.In an interview with Deutsche Welle published on Saturday, Zelenskyy said he would meet Putin if both leaders were invited to the Group of 20 summit of rich and developing nations in December in Miami.Putin's foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, said the possibility of Putin attending the summit had not yet been discussed.The Kremlin in the past has said that Zelenskyy can come to Moscow if he wants a meeting with Putin, a proposal Kyiv has rejected."If he really wants to meet with Putin, Putin has already said that he could fly to Moscow," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Saturday.Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov affirmed Saturday that Russia is "ready for negotiations," but that the so-called "special military operation," as Moscow refers to its war in Ukraine, "will not be suspended during this period of negotiations."On Wednesday, President Trump said he had a "great conversation" with Putin, and repeated his claim that he thinks the Russian leader wants to make a deal to end the war."He is wanting to make a deal," Mr. Trump said. "And if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that would be very nice."Mr. Trump has repeatedly said he thinks Putin wants to strike a deal to end the fighting, although the Russians could remove troops and relinquish territory at any point. A reporter asked the president what the holdup is. "The holdup is two people that hate each other," the president said. "I think more than anything else, it's two people that hate each other."
news.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that sending European troops into Ukraine would amount to direct conflict with Russia.
